entries.title: Atoms, the tiny pieces of matter
entries.answer: Air, water, rocks, and your own body are made of pieces called atoms. They are far too small to see with your eyes. An atom has a tiny center called a nucleus and electrons around it. The center holds particles called protons. The number of protons tells us what kind of atom it is. A hydrogen atom has one proton, and an oxygen atom has eight. Atoms can join together to make molecules. Different ways of joining a few kinds of atoms can give us materials with very different jobs.
facts: Electrons are much lighter than protons.
Most kinds of atoms also have neutrons in the nucleus.

entries.title: Density and why some things float
entries.answer: If you have two blocks the same size, one may feel much heavier. More matter is packed into that block’s space, so it is denser. A piece of wood often floats in water because the wood is less dense than the water. A big steel ship can float too. Its hollow shape gives it a lot of space without filling all that space with steel. The ship as a whole, with its air-filled spaces, has a lower average density than the water it pushes aside.
facts: Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats.
Salt water is denser than fresh water at the same temperature.

entries.title: How atoms join to make molecules
entries.answer: A molecule is a group of atoms joined together. One water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. Every water molecule has that same set of atoms, whether it is in a raindrop or a block of ice. Atoms of the same kind can join together too. The oxygen we breathe in has molecules made of two oxygen atoms. A molecule’s size, shape, and kinds of atoms help decide what it does. Some have just a few atoms, and others have thousands.
facts: H₂O is a short way to write what is in a water molecule.
Some molecules have just two atoms.

entries.title: How can a color show whether something is acidic?
entries.answer: Some coloring substances take on different colors in acidic and basic liquids. We call a substance used this way an indicator. A purple color from red cabbage, for instance, can become pinker in an acidic liquid and take on a different color in a basic one. Acidic and basic conditions change the structure of some of its color molecules. A color comparison can give a useful clue about pH, even if both liquids started out clear.
facts: Some indicators can show more than two colors across the pH scale.

entries.title: How can graphite and diamond both be carbon?
entries.answer: A piece of graphite and a diamond can both be made of carbon atoms. In graphite, carbon atoms connect in layers. Layers near the surface can slide and leave gray marks on a page. In diamond, the carbon atoms join in a firm pattern that runs in all directions. That pattern makes diamond hard to scratch. The element can stay the same even when the material’s color, feel and ability to scratch other things change a lot.
facts: Pencil “lead” usually contains graphite mixed with clay instead of lead metal.

questions.text: What makes the atoms in graphite and diamond belong to the same element?

entries.title: How can sand become glass?
entries.answer: A lot of familiar glass starts with sand rich in a material called silica. Glassmakers add other ingredients and heat the mix until it can flow. They shape it while it is hot, then cool it until it keeps its shape. The tiny particles inside do not settle into a neat repeating pattern, as they do in a salt crystal. Different ingredients and ways of shaping produce materials for windows, jars and much thinner objects, such as fine glass fibers.
facts: The glass in many bottles starts with silica sand and other ingredients.

entries.title: How can you tell a chemical reaction happened?
entries.answer: A chemical reaction happens when starting substances change into different substances. Their atoms are arranged in new ways. Perhaps you see a new color, see bubbles or feel a temperature change. Those signs can give a clue, but one sign by itself does not prove what happened. Soda can release bubbles that were already dissolved in it. By contrast, when iron rusts, part of the iron becomes a different substance that has a red-brown color and new properties.
facts: Atoms are rearranged during ordinary reactions rather than made from nothing.

entries.title: How does soft clay become a hard bowl?
entries.answer: Potters can shape damp clay before it dries, when its small particles can move past one another. Drying takes out water and helps the shape hold. Firing is a later step that heats the dried piece in a special oven called a kiln. The heat changes the material and bonds its particles. The new hard piece is a ceramic. If a potter adds a glaze, that coating can form a thin, glassy surface with its own color and shine.
facts: A kiln is an oven that can reach the heat needed to fire clay.

entries.title: How does stainless steel resist rust?
entries.answer: Stainless steel has iron mixed with enough of a metal called chromium to make a very thin protective layer on its surface. That layer forms when chromium meets oxygen. It helps keep air and moisture away from the metal underneath. A clean surface can often form a fresh protective layer after a small scratch. A spoon or sink made of stainless steel can stay bright through many washings. Some conditions, such as long contact with salt, can still damage it.
facts: Stainless steel can still corrode in some conditions.

entries.title: How is a compound different from a mixture?
entries.answer: A compound forms when atoms of different elements join in a fixed pattern or proportion. Water is a compound. Each water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. Mixing extra salt into water does not give a water molecule an extra atom. It makes a mixture with different kinds of particles sharing the same space. Some compounds, such as water, come in separate molecules. Others, such as ordinary table salt, can make repeating patterns with no single molecule to separate out.
facts: In each water molecule, two hydrogen atoms are joined to one oxygen atom.

questions.text: What is special about a material made of a single kind of atom?

entries.title: Solids, liquids, and gases
entries.answer: An ice cube, a puddle, and invisible water vapor are all made of water, but they act differently. In ice, the molecules stay in a pattern and jiggle around their spots. Ice is a solid and keeps its shape. In liquid water, the molecules slide past each other, so the water can flow and take the shape of its cup. In water vapor, the molecules can spread far apart. That is what makes it a gas. Adding or taking away heat can change water from one form to another.
facts: Melting changes solid ice into liquid water.
The same water molecules are still there when ice melts.

questions.text: What are the pieces that move around in water?
Why does water turn into drops inside a cloud?
Why does solid ice usually float in liquid water?

quiz.question: Which state of water takes the shape of the bottom of a cup and can be poured?
quiz.explanation: Liquid water flows while its molecules stay close together.

entries.title: What do pH numbers tell us?
entries.answer: pH is a way to describe how acidic or basic a water-based liquid is. Around room temperature, pure water is neutral and has a pH about 7. Lemon juice and vinegar are on the acidic side, with lower numbers. A liquid with a pH above 7 is on the basic side. Scientists can use an instrument or a substance that changes color to help check the pH. Two clear liquids can have quite different pH values.
facts: Near room temperature, pure water has a pH close to 7.

questions.text: How can one liquid’s color help reveal whether another is acidic?

entries.title: What makes a neon sign glow?
entries.answer: A real neon tube contains a small amount of neon gas. Electricity gives energy to atoms of that gas. When those atoms release some energy again, the light they give off looks reddish orange. The shape of the curved glass tube can turn that glow into letters or a picture. Other gases and special coatings can give similar signs different colors. A bright green sign may be called a neon sign in everyday speech even if its light does not mainly come from neon gas.
facts: Some signs called neon signs use different gases to make other colors.

questions.text: How can a gas such as neon belong to a single element?
How can a manufacturer shape material into a glass tube?
What can make one glowing object look like a different color from another?

entries.title: What makes something a chemical element
entries.answer: A chemical element is a kind of substance made of atoms that all have the same number of protons. Every gold atom has 79 protons, so a very pure piece of gold has atoms of just one element. A drop of pure water is different. Its molecules have atoms of two elements, hydrogen and oxygen, linked together. Scientists can arrange the elements in a chart called the periodic table. Two letters or one letter usually stand for each element on that chart. O stands for oxygen, and Au stands for gold.
facts: Carbon atoms all have six protons.
Iron is an element, but rust contains iron joined to other elements.

questions.text: Where in an atom are its protons?
How do atoms of different elements join together?

entries.title: What makes something a mixture?
entries.answer: A bowl with rice and beans holds a mixture. You can add more of either food and still recognize the pieces. Mixtures can be harder to see, too. Salt may spread out in water until both parts look like one clear liquid. The amount of salt can change from one glass to another. With a pure substance like water, molecules of that substance always have the same set of atoms. Some mixtures look even all the way through. Others have parts you can see.
facts: You can change the amount of one ingredient in a mixture.

questions.text: How can a substance stay in a mixture after you stop seeing it?

Why do some combined liquids form separate layers?

entries.title: Where does sugar go when it dissolves?
entries.answer: When sugar dissolves, it is still there even after you stop seeing the grains. Water separates the sugar molecules from the grain and surrounds them without breaking apart the individual molecules. The tiny sugar molecules spread throughout the water, making an even mixture called a solution. Stirring moves less sugary water toward the grains and carries sugar away from them. If you let the water leave as vapor, some of the dissolved material can collect as solid again. Dissolving sugar is different from changing it into another substance.
facts: Stirring can help sugar dissolve faster.

questions.text: What happens if you keep adding sugar after the water is full of dissolved sugar?
How can dissolved sugar or salt become solid again?
Why does oil behave differently in water?

entries.title: Why can baking soda make batter rise?
entries.answer: Baking soda can react with a food acid in wet batter and release carbon dioxide gas. The gas makes little bubbles that take up room. In an oven, the batter can set around those bubbles, leaving open spaces and making the baked food feel lighter. If the recipe uses a different source of gas, the spaces can look similar even though the gas formed in a different way. Bread made with yeast can hold carbon dioxide, too.
facts: Carbon dioxide is the gas in bubbles made when baking soda reacts with an acid.

questions.text: How do the starting substances change as they release gas?
How does yeast make gas in a different way?
How is the gas in a fizzy drink similar?

entries.title: Why can plastics feel so different?
entries.answer: A lot of the material in plastic is made from very long molecules. Such molecules may form loose chains or a tighter network. Their size, shape and links affect how far they can move and bend. Manufacturers can also add other ingredients. A squeeze bottle needs to bend under your fingers. A toy part might need to keep its shape. Both could be plastic even though one feels soft and the other feels hard, because their ingredients and structures can differ.
facts: Many plastics can soften when warmed and harden again when cooled.

questions.text: What can a number on a plastic bottle tell you about its material?
How can made fibers differ from cotton or wool fibers?
What can change when the ingredients of a solid material change?

entries.title: Why do crystals have neat shapes?
entries.answer: In a crystal, very small particles fit together in a pattern that repeats. Adding more particles in matching positions can grow that same pattern outward. The resulting solid may have flat faces or sharp edges that reflect its inner arrangement. Some salt grains look like tiny boxes when you see them through a magnifier. A broken crystal may have chipped or uneven edges, but its remaining particles still follow a pattern. Crystals can grow from melted, dissolved or gaseous materials in suitable conditions.
facts: Even a crystal too small to study with your eyes has a repeating arrangement inside.

questions.text: How can a liquid mixture end up holding more dissolved material than it can keep?
How does a regular pattern make ice take up more space?
How is the pattern inside glass different from a crystal?

entries.title: Why do water drops hold together?
entries.answer: Water molecules tug on other water molecules near them. A molecule deep in water is pulled from many directions. A molecule at the surface has much less water above it, so the surface tends to draw tight. This is called surface tension. It helps make a small drop round rather than spread very far. When the conditions are right, a small insect can stand on top of water without breaking through, with its feet making little dents in the surface.
facts: Soap can lower the surface tension of clean water.

questions.text: How does soap let water stretch into a film around air?
How does soap change the way water meets a greasy surface?
How does water sticking to itself help a plant move water upward?

entries.title: Why does an old nail turn rusty?
entries.answer: Iron can slowly react with oxygen when water is present. Some of the iron becomes new compounds containing iron and oxygen. We see these as red-brown rust. Rust can form rough flakes, leaving more iron underneath open to air and moisture. Salty water often helps the process go faster. Paint and some other coatings can protect an iron object if they keep air and water from touching the metal. A dry object can stay in better shape for much longer.
facts: A coating that keeps water and air away can help protect iron.

entries.title: Why does extra sugar stay on the bottom?
entries.answer: At a given temperature, a glass of water can hold only a certain amount of dissolved sugar. When it holds as much as it can, the solution is saturated. Extra sugar can remain as grains at the bottom even after plenty of stirring. Warming water often lets it hold more sugar, though not every substance responds to temperature in the same way. When a concentrated sugar solution cools, it may no longer be able to hold all that sugar in the water.
facts: A saturated solution can still look clear above any extra solid.

How can a dissolved substance begin forming solid patterns?
What changes how much gas can stay dissolved in water?

entries.title: Why does ice float on liquid water?
entries.answer: In liquid water, molecules can move and slip close to one another. When ordinary ice forms, the molecules lock into a regular arrangement with more open space. The amount of water can stay the same while its solid form takes up more room. That makes ice less dense than liquid water. A piece of ice can float with some of itself above the surface and more of itself below. This is one reason pond ice forms at the top.
facts: The same amount of water takes up more space as ordinary ice than as liquid water.

entries.title: Why does water bubble when it boils?
entries.answer: As water heats, more of its molecules can move into a gas. At the boiling point, bubbles of water vapor can grow inside the liquid and reach the surface. Evaporation can happen just at the surface long before a pot boils. Air pressure around the water helps set its boiling point. Higher on a mountain, the pressure is lower, so water generally begins boiling at a lower temperature. Bubbling water can therefore be at different temperatures in different places.
facts: Water can boil at a lower temperature on a high mountain than near sea level.

questions.text: How can water leave a lake’s surface without boiling?

entries.title: Why don’t oil and water mix evenly?
entries.answer: In water, the parts of each molecule that pull on nearby molecules help water gather together. Oil molecules do not make the same strong connections with water. If you shake oil and water, some oil breaks into little drops, but the drops can bump into one another and join up again. Many cooking oils also have lower density than water, so their layer ends up on top. Floating and failing to dissolve are different effects. Both can happen in the same glass.
facts: Oil and water can look temporarily mixed right after shaking.

questions.text: Why is the layer of many cooking oils above the layer of water?
How can soap help break up a layer of oil?

entries.title: Why mix one metal with other elements?
entries.answer: An alloy contains at least one metal mixed with other elements. The mixture can behave differently from the pure metal. It might hold a shape better under pressure, be easier to work with, or be slower to react with air. Brass combines copper and zinc. Traditional bronze often adds tin to copper, while steel contains iron with some carbon. Different alloys fit different jobs. The metal in a musical instrument can have a different mix from the metal in a bicycle part.
facts: Brass commonly combines copper with zinc.
